content: Non-polio enteroviruses are a genus of positive-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses that are associated with a variety of diseases in humans and other mammals. Serologic studies have identified 66 human enterovirus serotypes based on antibody neutralization tests. Within these serotypes, additional antigenic variants have been defined due to reduced or nonreciprocal cross-neutralization between variant strains. Enteroviruses were initially classified into four groups based on their pathogenicity in humans and animals: polioviruses, Coxsackie A viruses (CA), Coxsackie B viruses (CB), and echoviruses. However, it was soon recognized that there were significant overlaps in the biological properties of viruses within these groups. Non-polio enteroviruses are transmitted through direct contact with respiratory secretions (such as saliva, sputum, or nasal mucus) or stool from an infected individual. Infection can also occur through contact with contaminated surfaces or objects, such as drinking glasses or telephones. Parents, teachers, and childcare workers are at particular risk of infection due to hand contamination with stool from infected infants or toddlers during diaper changes. Non-polio enterovirus infections are caused by enteroviruses, which are composed of RNA and protein. This group includes polioviruses, Coxsackie viruses, echoviruses, and other enteroviruses. In addition to the three types of polioviruses, there are over 60 types of non-polio enteroviruses that can cause disease in humans. These viruses are extremely common and are second only to rhinoviruses (the viruses responsible for the common cold) as the most frequent viral infectious agents in humans. Non-polio enteroviruses are responsible for an estimated 10–15 million or more symptomatic infections annually in the United States. However, all three types of polioviruses have been eradicated from the Western Hemisphere, as well as the Western Pacific and European regions, due to widespread vaccination efforts. Parents, teachers, and childcare workers are particularly susceptible to non-polio enterovirus infections because they may come into contact with stool from infected infants or toddlers during diaper changes. Although everyone is at risk of infection, certain factors, such as age and season, can increase the likelihood of contracting non-polio enteroviruses. Most individuals infected with a non-polio enterovirus remain asymptomatic. Those who do develop symptoms typically experience mild upper respiratory symptoms (commonly referred to as a summer cold), a flu-like illness with fever and muscle aches, or an illness accompanied by a rash.
